what_its_for: Enoxaparin is a blood thinner (anticoagulant) that helps prevent and treat dangerous blood clots. It is used to prevent clots after surgery (especially hip, knee, or stomach surgery), to treat deep vein thrombosis (DVT, a clot in your leg), pulmonary embolism (a clot in your lungs), and to help prevent clots in people with certain heart conditions like unstable chest pain or heart attack.
how_to_take: Enoxaparin is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in the belly area (abdomen). Do not inject into muscle. Each dose comes in a prefilled syringe. Choose a spot at least 2 inches away from your belly button. Pinch a fold of skin, insert the needle at a 45 to 90 degree angle, push the plunger all the way down, and then release the skin. Do not rub the injection site after giving the shot, as this can cause bruising. Rotate injection sites each time to avoid skin irritation. Your nurse or doctor will teach you how to give yourself this injection at home.
dosing: Your dose depends on your weight, kidney function, and what condition is being treated. Common doses range from 30 mg to 1 mg per kilogram of body weight, given once or twice daily. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions. Do not change your dose on your own. If you are unsure about your dose, call your doctor or pharmacist.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, inject it as soon as you remember, unless it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never inject two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist right away.
storage: Store enoxaparin at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and freezing temperatures. Do not put it in the freezer. Keep all syringes out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of used needles and syringes in a puncture-resistant sharps container. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of your sharps container.
what_to_avoid: Avoid activities that could cause cuts, bruises, or injury while taking this medication, as you will bleed more easily. Avoid contact sports or rough activities. Do not take aspirin, ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) unless your doctor tells you it is safe. Avoid alcohol in large amounts. Do not start any new prescription or over-the-counter medications, vitamins, or herbal supplements without first checking with your doctor or pharmacist.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room immediately if you notice: unusual or heavy bleeding (such as from cuts, gums, or nose that won't stop), blood in your urine (pink, red, or dark brown color), blood in your stool (red or black, tarry stools), vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, coughing up blood, unusual bruising, severe headache, dizziness, or weakness, numbness or tingling in your legs or feet (especially if you have had a spinal procedure), or chest pain or trouble breathing. Also call your doctor before any dental procedures, surgery, or if you become pregnant.
when_it_works: Enoxaparin starts working to thin your blood within 1 to 2 hours after your injection. You will not feel it working, but it is actively preventing or treating clots during this time. It is very important to use it exactly as prescribed and not miss doses to keep your blood at the right level of thinness.
special_populations: Older adults (over 65): You may have a higher risk of bleeding. Your doctor may monitor you more closely or adjust your dose. Kidney problems: If your kidneys do not work well, the drug can build up in your body and increase bleeding risk. Your doctor will likely lower your dose and monitor you carefully. Pregnancy: Enoxaparin does not cross the placenta and is considered safer than some other blood thinners during pregnancy, but always tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Children: Dosing in children is based on weight and must be determined by a doctor. Low body weight (under 45 kg or 99 lbs): You may need a lower dose to avoid bleeding complications.
